Volume 14 · Chapter 05

New Keynesian models and monetary policy

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c04

By the endDerive a nominal-rigidity model and compare policy rules under explicit approximations.

Volume 14 · Chapter 5

New Keynesian models and monetary policy

A central bank announces a stronger response to inflation. Does that select one equilibrium, reduce a particular shock’s effects, or improve welfare? These are three different questions. We derive a price-setting economy, identify exactly what its linear approximation retains, and solve policy examples whose roots and conditional expectations can be checked.

Capability. Derive CES demand, an optimizing Calvo reset price, price dispersion, the first-order Phillips and IS equations, and a qualified determinacy result. Compare rules and diagnose a rate floor without presenting a local model as an exact nonlinear equilibrium or a policy recommendation.

Prerequisites. Recursive methods supplies conditional Euler and terminal reasoning; Stochastic growth distinguishes equilibrium from approximation. Search and labor dynamics studies a different labor-market friction. Here labor is competitively allocated and nominal goods prices are sticky; search unemployment is not silently imported. Two-by-two characteristic roots, conditional expectations and geometric series are reviewed where needed.

Every parameter, shock and numerical economy below is synthetic. A period is not assigned a calendar frequency. In particular, the rational benchmark’s discount factor and Phillips slope were chosen for transparent arithmetic, not estimated from a national economy.

1. Households, differentiated goods and funded subsidies

There is a representative household, a continuum of goods j∈[0,1], no capital, no government consumption and no trade. Productivity At>0 is observed before decisions. Aggregate shocks have finite support at each finite history; conditional expectations Et use their true law. Choices are adapted to current information. The household owns every firm and supplies a homogeneous labor input N≥0. Unlike the leisure specification in Chapter 2, this model uses convex labor disutility without an hours ceiling:

E₀∑ βᵗ[U(C_t)−χN_t^(1+φ)/(1+φ)],   U′(C)=C^(−σ),   0<β<1, σ>0, φ>0, χ>0.

For σ=1, U=log C; otherwise take U(C)=C1−σ/(1−σ). Consumption is the CES aggregate C=[∫C(j)(ε−1)/εdj]ε/(ε−1), with substitution elasticity ε>1. Given prices, cost minimization for a specified C gives P(j)=ΛC(j)−1/εC1/ε. Taking ratios and substituting back into the aggregator yields

C_t(j)=[P_t(j)/P_t]^(−ε)C_t,   P_t=[∫P_t(j)^(1−ε)dj]^[1/(1−ε)],   ∫P_t(j)C_t(j)dj=P_tC_t.

These are global expenditure-minimizing demands, not just stationary equations: the CES aggregator is concave and its supporting gradient at the proposed bundle is proportional to the price vector, so any bundle reaching the same aggregate consumption costs at least as much. Strict convexity of the dual choice on positive goods gives the usual unique demands up to null goods. Assume positive finite price integrals throughout.

A nominal discount bond purchased for QtBt+1 at t pays Bt+1 at t+1; the gross nominal return is Rt=1/Qt. The household budget is

P_tC_t+Q_tB_(t+1)≤B_t+W_tN_t+D_t−T_t.

D denotes distributed firm profits and T lump-sum taxes. Bonds are in zero net supply and the representative equilibrium has B=0. Individual admissible deviations must satisfy their budget and a no-Ponzi restriction; in present-value form at the candidate nominal stochastic discount factor, require liminf E₀[Mnom0,TQTBT+1]≥0. An optimum with no terminal bequest has equality. Here Mnom0,T=βT(CT/C0)−σP0/PT. This restriction is part of the admissible class, not a conclusion from Euler equations. We derive interior necessary conditions and a local equilibrium system; we do not claim a global nonlinear household-existence theorem for every price process.

Finite labor and two-date bond perturbations at a finite-valued interior optimum give

W_t/P_t=χC_t^σN_t^φ,   Q_t=βE_t[(C_(t+1)/C_t)^(−σ)P_t/P_(t+1)].

The bond costs Q today and pays one tomorrow, explaining its timing and the price ratio. Conditional returns belong inside expectations. A borrowing limit would replace the bond equality by its relevant one-sided condition and would change the model.

Firm j produces Y(j)=AN(j) and sells to CES demand. A proportional subsidy τ∈[0,1) reimburses part of its wage bill, so its nominal marginal cost is M=(1−τ)W/A. Government levies the contemporaneous lump-sum tax T=τWN, funding exactly the subsidy. Profits are D=PY−(1−τ)WN, and therefore WN+D−T=PY. Adding a subsidy to profits while omitting its taxes would manufacture household resources. Goods-market clearing implies C=Y.

With flexible prices the desired markup is μ=ε/(ε−1) and P=μM. The choice τ=1/ε removes the steady monopoly wedge, because μ(1−τ)=1. Then flexible-price real wages equal A and the flexible allocation coincides with the efficient one within these primitives. Without that subsidy, the natural flexible-price allocation is distorted; a zero output gap relative to it is not automatically efficient. We retain the funded correcting subsidy below.

Method source: Jordi Galí, The Basic New Keynesian Model, May 2018, numbered slides 4–11 and 13–16. Its household, Calvo and local policy framework guides the methods. We specialize to linear production, supply our own funded-subsidy accounts, proofs and examples, and use an output-gap rule rather than silently equating the source’s output-level rule with it.

2. Exact Calvo pricing and the resources lost to dispersion

At each date a fraction 1−θ of firms may reset their nominal price, independently of their age or aggregate shocks, with 0<θ<1. A price survives j more periods with probability θj. Assume the continuum has these exact fractions. Nonresetters keep their nominal price without indexation; symmetric resetters choose the same P*t. Firms are atomistic and take aggregate demand, wages and discount factors as given. With linear production, marginal cost does not depend on an individual firm’s output.

The conditional reset objective, measured in date-t household consumption units, is the expected discounted profit stream while that price survives:

∑_(j≥0)(βθ)^j E_t{(C_(t+j)/C_t)^(−σ)[P*−M_(t+j)](P*/P_(t+j))^(−ε)Y_(t+j)/P_(t+j)}.

Assume its positive coefficient sums below are finite, permitting differentiation; for example bounded positive aggregate prices, consumption, output and costs bounded away from zero suffice. Define S₀=∑(βθ)jEt[Ct+j−σYt+jPt+jε−1] and S₁ with an additional factor Mt+j. Dropping the positive common factor Ctσ, profit is S₀(P*)1−ε−S₁(P*)−ε. Its derivative has the sign of εS₁−(ε−1)S₀P*. Thus

P*=μS₁/S₀.

This is the unique global optimum on P*>0: profit increases below this point, decreases above it, tends to −∞ at zero, and tends to zero at infinity. This conditional firm proof is exact. It does not prove that arbitrary input paths for wages and aggregate demand form a general equilibrium. Calvo’s hazard changes how long a resetter internalizes future costs; its first-order price response is not based solely on today’s marginal cost.

Let Πt=Pt/Pt−1 and r*t=P*t/Pt. The CES index and Calvo population accounting imply the exact identities

1=θΠ_t^(ε−1)+(1−θ)(r*_t)^(1−ε),
Δ_t=θΠ_t^εΔ_(t−1)+(1−θ)(r*_t)^(−ε),   Δ_t≡∫[P_t(j)/P_t]^(−ε)dj,
N_t=(Y_t/A_t)Δ_t.

To see why Δ≥1, let X(j)=[P(j)/P]1−ε. The price index makes ∫X=1, while Δ=∫Xε/(ε−1). Strict convexity and Jensen’s inequality imply Δ≥1, with equality only for uniform prices almost everywhere. Dispersion uses extra labor for the same CES output. Average physical units across unlike varieties are not the CES final good.

Worked case 1. Nominal prices that require extra real resources

Half the firms charge an inherited price one and half reset to three halves. Let (θ,ε,Pold,Preset,Y,A)=(1/2,2,1,3/2,1,1). This is an exact accounting snapshot, not a claim that these prices solve a policy equilibrium. The index is P=[(1/2)/1+(1/2)/(3/2)]−1=6/5. Demands per old and resetting firm are (36/25,16/25). Half of each produces final CES output one but total labor 26/25.

Expenditure is (1/2)(1)(36/25)+(1/2)(3/2)(16/25)=6/5=PY. Relative reset price is 5/4, gross inflation is 6/5, and the recursion from Δ−1=1 gives Δ=(1/2)(6/5)²+(1/2)(5/4)−2=26/25. Uniform prices could produce the same aggregate good with labor one. The extra four percent is a resource comparison within this snapshot, not an estimated welfare loss or an assertion about observed inflation.

Worked case 2. An anticipated cost increase enters the reset price

In a conditional price-setting problem, set (β,θ,ε,M0,Mfuture)=(4/5,1/2,2,2/5,3/5), with C=Y=P=1 at all dates. Current nominal marginal cost is 2/5; at every future date it is 3/5. These are supplied atomistic-firm input paths, not a separately demonstrated equilibrium. The survival-adjusted discount is βθ=2/5. Geometric sums give S₀=5/3 and S₁=2/5+(3/5)(2/5)/(1−2/5)=4/5. The reset price is 24/25, above today’s desired flexible price 4/5 and below the future desired price 6/5.

The normalized profit is (5/3)/p−(4/5)/p². At p=24/25 it equals 125/144; at p=4/5 it is 5/6. The derivative-sign proof establishes global optimality beyond these comparisons. If the firm’s objective genuinely ended after tomorrow, the sums would instead be 7/5 and 16/25, yielding price 32/35. Truncating an infinite reset stream and forgetting its remainder solves a different firm problem.

3. What the first-order approximation keeps

Expand around a deterministic zero-inflation steady state with uniform prices, the constant correcting subsidy and no financial constraint. Write lower-case y,c,n,a for log deviations of output, consumption, labor and productivity from that state, π=logΠ, and i=logR−ī for the nominal-rate deviation, where ī=−logβ>0. These i and π are log rates per model period, not annualized percentages. The expansion assumes a differentiable family of nearby allocations, positive consumption, and domination permitting linearization of the expected discounted price sums. We derive its necessary equations; existence of a nearby exact nonlinear equilibrium is an additional question.

At first order, the index gives p*−p=θπ/(1−θ). Differentiating the dispersion recursion around Δ=1 gives dΔt=θdΔt−1+θεπ−(1−θ)ε(p*−p)=θdΔt−1. If initial dispersion has no first-order deviation, it remains absent at this order, so n=y−a and c=y. This does not make exact dispersion zero. A distribution with an independently nonzero first-order dispersion state is not covered by that two-variable approximation.

Let m be the deviation of log real marginal cost M/P from log(1/μ). In the price ratio S₁/S₀, first-order changes in common weighting factors cancel around the constant desired price. The log reset price therefore satisfies p*=(1−βθ)(p+m)+βθEtp*t+1. Equivalently q*≡p*−p obeys q*=(1−βθ)m+βθE(q*′+π′). Substituting the price-index relation gives

π_t=βE_tπ_(t+1)+λm_t,   λ=(1−θ)(1−βθ)/θ.

One can also derive this from the geometric weighted-average reset price and verify the vanished terminal term under a bounded local continuation restriction. Without such a restriction a forward equation alone can carry an extra explosive solution. The formula presumes 0<θ<1. At θ=0 flexible pricing is handled directly, not by substituting into a division by zero; at θ=1 there are no resetters and this reset problem no longer applies.

The labor condition and linear production yield m=σy+φn−a=(σ+φ)y−(1+φ)a. Under flexible prices m=0. Thus natural output relative to its steady level is yn=[(1+φ)/(σ+φ)]a. Here it is also efficient output because the subsidy corrects the monopoly wedge. Define the economic output gap x=y−yn. The Phillips curve becomes

π_t=βE_tπ_(t+1)+κx_t,   κ=λ(σ+φ)>0.

The gap is not output minus a statistical trend. A productivity improvement changes natural output; stabilizing the gap need not stabilize the level of output. Variable markups, wage frictions or a changed subsidy can add a pricing wedge, but those are additional primitives and are absent from this baseline.

Linearizing the exact bond Euler equation gives y=E y′−(i−Eπ′)/σ. In terms of the gap,

x_t=E_tx_(t+1)−[i_t−E_tπ_(t+1)−r_t^n]/σ,   r_t^n≡σE_t(y_(t+1)^n−y_t^n).

rn is the deviation of the natural real rate; its level is ī+rn at first order. Expected inflation is subtracted from the nominal rate with the same timing. Risk corrections to a nonlinear expected gross return are higher-order terms, not an exact Jensen-free identity. A mean-reverting positive productivity level can increase current natural output while lowering expected natural growth and hence rn.

For the rational benchmark (β,θ,σ,φ)=(4/5,1/2,1,1), λ=3/5 and κ=6/5. These large illustrative coefficients make the following roots exact; no empirical fit is intended.

4. A rule, a root count and a precise uniqueness class

Consider the contemporaneous rule i=φππ+φxx+ν, where ν is an exogenous rate-rule intercept disturbance. Initially assume φπ,φx≥0, no rate floor, and the model’s stated true conditional expectations. There is no interest-rate smoothing, capital, habit or price indexation. The two endogenous variables x,π can both jump. The initial price level fixes nominal units; inherited dispersion has no first-order deviation. Exogenous shock states are predetermined but are supplied by their own law, not counted as extra endogenous jump variables.

For z=(x,π)′, solving the Phillips equation for expected inflation and then the IS equation for expected output gives

E_tz_(t+1)=Az_t+f_t,
A=[[1+φ_x/σ+κ/(σβ), (φ_π−1/β)/σ], [−κ/β,1/β]],   f_t=((ν_t−r_t^n)/σ,0)′.

The convention matters: A maps current variables into expected future variables. Two roots outside the unit circle select bounded solutions for two jump variables. If instead one writes current variables as A−1 times expected future variables, the corresponding roots must be inside. Reporting a root without its matrix convention is ambiguous.

Proposition and proof. In this two-equation system with 0<β<1, σ,κ>0 and nonnegative rule coefficients, exactly two roots of A lie outside the unit circle if and only if

κ(φ_π−1)+(1−β)φ_x>0.

Let T=tr A=1+φx/σ+(1+κ/σ)/β>2 and D=det A=[1+φx/σ+κφπ/σ]/β>1. The characteristic polynomial is p(ℓ)=ℓ²−Tℓ+D, with p(1)=[κ(φπ−1)+(1−β)φx]/(σβ). If roots are complex conjugates, each has modulus √D>1 and p(1)=|1−ℓ|²>0. If roots are real, T,D>0 imply both positive. For p(1)>0 they lie on the same side of one; T>2 excludes both below it. If p(1)<0, one lies in (0,1) and the other above one. At equality one root is exactly one and the other D>1. This proves the criterion and its boundary under the maintained sign restrictions.

What uniqueness means here. Suppose f is uniformly bounded over dates and histories, and seek uniformly bounded adapted rational-expectations solutions. The filtration may include additional public random signals independent of fundamental shocks; conditional expectations remain objective. If both roots of A exceed one in modulus, M=A−1 has powers tending geometrically to zero, allowing a polynomial factor for a repeated root. Iteration yields the unique bounded solution

z_t=−∑_(j≥0)M^(j+1)E_tf_(t+j).

The series converges absolutely in a matrix norm and satisfies the equation by the tower property. To prove uniqueness, subtract two solutions: dt=MnEtdt+n. Their uniform bound and Mn→0 imply d=0. This eliminates bounded additional sunspot-driven solutions within the stated class; it does not exclude every unbounded or nonintegrable process or prove global nonlinear uniqueness. With a stable real eigenvalue ℓ∈(0,1), a deterministic addition cℓtv to any bounded solution is another bounded solution for every sufficiently small c. A unit eigenvalue similarly permits a constant addition. Even without constructing stochastic sunspots, those additions disprove uniqueness.

Worked case 3. Active, passive and boundary rules

Use the rational benchmark and (φπ,φx)=(3/2,1/2). The forward matrix is ((3,1/4),(-3/2,5/4)), with (trace,determinant)=(17/4,33/8) and roots (3/2,11/4). Both endogenous variables jump, so bounded equilibrium is unique. The inequality margin is κ/2+(1/5)/2=7/10>0.

With (φπ,φx)=(1/4,0), the roots are (1/2,13/4). At zero fundamental shocks, zt=c(1/2)t(1/2,1)′ is a continuum of bounded equilibria. At the boundary (φπ,φx)=(1,0), roots are (1,11/4); any constant (x,π)=(c/6,c) solves the zero-shock equations. Strict inequality is essential. Positive feedback to the gap can also permit φπ below one; “inflation coefficient above one” is a sufficient shortcut here, not the full condition.

A usable numerical certificate. For the active rule, M=((10/33,-2/33),(4/11,8/11)). Its ordinary maximum absolute row sum is 12/11>1, so that norm does not give a contraction. Let S=[[1,1],[−1,−6]], whose columns are eigenvectors of A, and use ‖v‖S=‖S−1v‖∞. Then ‖M‖S=2/3. If a bounded candidate has residual et=z̃t−MEtz̃t+1+Mft with sup‖e‖S≤η, its distance from the exact linear solution is at most 3η in this norm. Iterating the error equation proves the bound; rows of S give coordinate bounds |Δx|≤6η and |Δπ|≤21η. A residual computed with a wrong expectation law or discretized operator needs an additional error bound. This certificate concerns the stated linear model, not nonlinear welfare.

5. Solve the shock before interpreting a policy coefficient

Let ν have conditional persistence Etνt+1=ρνt, |ρ|<1, and set rn=0. A bounded two-state process with values ±v and stay probability (1+ρ)/2 is one explicit implementation. Seek x=Xν and π=Hν. The Phillips curve gives H=κX/(1−βρ). The IS equation and rule then imply

X=−1/D_ρ,   H=−κ/[(1−βρ)D_ρ],
D_ρ=σ(1−ρ)+φ_x+(φ_π−ρ)κ/(1−βρ).

This is a candidate particular solution. Under the determinacy conditions above it is the unique bounded solution; under a passive rule, solving these coefficients would not rule out additional homogeneous solutions. The same formulas with the opposite sign apply to a natural-rate disturbance of the same persistence when ν=0. Nominal-rate effects must be calculated using the equilibrium feedbacks, not read from the coefficient one on ν.

Worked case 4. A contractionary intercept whose observed nominal rate falls

Use the active rule and benchmark coefficients, with (ρ,ν)=(1/2,3/100). Then κ/(1−βρ)=2 and Dρ=3. The current solution is (x,π,i)=(-1/100,-1/50,-1/200). Expected next inflation is −1/100; the ex-ante real-rate deviation i−Eπ′ is 1/200, which contracts demand. The nominal rate falls because expected inflation and endogenous feedback fall enough to offset the positive intercept. Calling a positive ν an observed nominal-rate increase would confuse an equation’s intervention with its equilibrium outcome.

Now strengthen only φπ from 3/2 to 2, retaining φx=1/2. Dρ=4 and the response is (x,π,i)=(-3/400,-3/200,-3/800). Both gap and inflation magnitudes shrink by one quarter for this particular shock and persistence. That comparison is not an optimal-policy theorem: a different disturbance, welfare criterion, information set or floor can change the ranking.

For contrast, keep the original rule but make the same ν=3/100 iid, so ρ=0. The solution is (x,π,i)=(-1/110,-3/275,1/110). Here expected next gap and inflation are zero and the nominal rate rises. Persistence is part of the experiment. These are conditional first-order log responses, not an exact nonlinear impulse response in percentage levels.

If the authority could observe the true natural rate and implement i=rn+φππ+φxx without a floor, then x=π=0 is a solution and is the unique bounded one under the same determinacy condition. Actual output would equal moving natural output, not remain constant. In this undistorted no-cost-push benchmark, inflation and efficient-gap stabilization are compatible. That compatibility is conditional on the correcting subsidy, information, feasibility and missing distortions; it does not prove every real stabilization policy improves welfare.

6. A rate floor changes the equations and the solution test

Suppose a nominal lower bound requires logR≥0. Since i is a deviation, its lower bound is −ī=logβ, not zero. A piecewise rule is i=max{−ī,φππ+φxx+ν}. When the floor binds, the local feedback coefficients governing the active region no longer describe the current regime. The previous infinite-horizon uniqueness theorem cannot simply be applied to a path that crosses this kink.

Worked case 5. An announced two-date disturbance at the floor

For this separate first-order economy take (β,σ,κ,φπ,φx,r)=(99/100,1,1/10,2,1,-1/50). κ is a stipulated positive local slope, compatible with a suitable Calvo duration and positive preference curvatures; it is not the earlier benchmark’s 6/5. Set ν=0, ī=−log(99/100)≈0.01005033585350145. Natural-rate deviations equal r for t=0,1 and zero thereafter. The terminal selection is x2=π2=0, with the zero continuation for every t≥2. Everyone knows this two-date path. We solve this finite-horizon conditional experiment, not every possible infinite-horizon floor equilibrium.

At t=1, if the floor binds, i1=−ī and x1=r+ī, π1=κx1. Numerically (x1,π1,i1)=(-0.00994966414649855,-0.000994966414649855,-0.01005033585350145). The desired unfloored rate is (1+2κ)x1=1.2x1≈−0.01193960, below the floor. Thus the assumed regime is consistent. The nominal rate level is logR=0, even though its deviation i is negative.

At t=0, the common known continuation gives x0=x1−[−ī−π1−r]=(2+κ)x1 and π0=βπ1+κx0. The result is (x0,π0,i0)=(-0.020894294707646956,-0.003074446221268052,-0.01005033585350145). Its shadow rule rate 2π0+x0 is again below −ī. Expected deflation tomorrow raises today’s real borrowing cost at a fixed nominal floor, amplifying the gap.

For completeness, fix any continuation (x′,π′). Let B=x′+(π′+r)/σ and π=βπ′+κx. The IS equation says x=B−i/σ. Substituting the rule gives a continuous scalar equation

x+(1/σ)max{−ī,φπβπ′+(φx+φπκ)x+ν}=B.

Under the positive coefficients in this case, its left side is strictly increasing from −∞ to +∞. Hence each date has exactly one solution for its fixed continuation. Backward induction proves uniqueness of this finite-terminal experiment, not a global stationary determinacy result. If one instead forces the unfloored rate at date one, i≈−0.01090909 violates the nominal floor; a small equation residual inside the wrong regime does not rescue feasibility.

The first-order economy is itself an approximation. Two percent log-gap responses and the zero-rate kink merit nonlinear validation before quantitative use. Neither the three residuals nor this conditional backward proof supplies an error bound for an exact Calvo economy, a fiscal financing rule, or a welfare optimum.

7. Exercises that separate optimization, approximation and selection

  1. Derive CES demand and the price index by expenditure minimization. In case 1 compute expenditure, dispersion and labor both directly and from the Calvo recursion. Prove Δ≥1 and explain why summing physical output across varieties is not final output.
  2. Prove that the ratio μS₁/S₀ is the unique global reset-price maximizer when 0<S₀,S₁<∞. Reconstruct both the infinite and genuinely two-date prices in case 2. Give the missing infinite continuation sums after date one and explain why a two-date truncation is not merely a harmless numerical stopping rule.
  3. Differentiate the exact price-index and dispersion recursions around uniform prices and zero inflation. State the initial-distribution condition needed to remove dispersion from the first-order resource equation. If instead a separate admissible initialization has dΔ₋₁=d>0, derive dΔt and identify the additional predetermined state.
  4. Derive the household Euler equation with the stated discount-bond timing, then the IS equation and natural-rate definition. Set (σ,φ,ρa,a)=(2,1,4/5,3/100) and Eta′=ρaa. Find current natural output and natural real-rate deviation. Explain why a positive productivity level need not raise that rate.
  5. Derive the NK Phillips coefficient from the reset and price-index equations. Keep β=4/5,σ=φ=1 but change θ to 3/4. Compute λ and κ, compare κ with the benchmark and state why the limits θ=0 and θ=1 need separate economic treatment.
  6. Prove the determinacy condition under the stated nonnegative policy coefficients using trace, determinant and p(1). Compute the roots for the three case-3 rules. Verify the passive decaying eigenvector and the unit-root constant solutions. State the filtration and boundedness class over which the uniqueness claim is proved.
  7. Keep the rational benchmark and inflation coefficient 3/2 but set -5/2 for φx. Compute the forward matrix and both characteristic roots. Does an inflation coefficient above one now establish uniqueness? Explain why counting two jump variables changes the interpretation of two stable roots.
  8. Derive the undetermined coefficients X,H for the bounded persistent rule shock. Reconstruct the persistent, stronger-rule and iid responses in case 4. Compute expected next inflation and the ex-ante real-rate deviation in all three cases; reconcile each with the IS equation. Does the nominal-rate sign identify the structural intercept shock?
  9. Under i=rn+φππ+φxx, prove that zero inflation and zero gap are the unique bounded allocation deviations when the active-rule conditions hold. Explain why actual output still moves with productivity. Now remove the subsidy correction: distinguish natural output, efficient output and the welfare interpretation of stabilizing their respective gaps.
  10. In the one-date version of case 5, with zero continuation, derive the exact threshold in r below which the floor binds. Compute both regimes and verify the two-date solution by backward induction. Explain why setting the deviation i to zero does not mean a zero nominal rate, and why the calculation is not a theorem about all infinite-horizon floor equilibria.
  11. For the active benchmark, verify the matrix M=A−1, the eigenvector matrix S and S−1. Prove the bounded-candidate residual certificate in ‖·‖S, including the coordinate bounds. At 1/100000, report bounds for x and π. Explain why using the ordinary row-sum norm would not justify a contraction and why a wrong shock law needs separate control.
  12. Referee: “The Taylor coefficient exceeds one, our simulated Euler residuals are tiny, and the output gap uses detrended GDP. Therefore the exact economy has one equilibrium and this policy is socially optimal even at the lower bound.” Supply four explicit objections, a relevant calculation or counterexample for each, and a minimal replacement claim. Include policy funding, model-versus-data identification and the approximation’s scope. Use the ten-point rubric in the solution.
Complete solutions and referee rubric

  1. The CES gradient is C1/εC(j)−1/ε. The cost-minimizing first-order conditions set P(j) proportional to that gradient, so C(j)=K P(j)−ε. Substitution into the CES constraint gives K=C[∫P(j)1−εdj]ε/(1−ε)=CPε. Substituting these demands into expenditure yields PC. Global optimality follows from the concave aggregator’s supporting inequality: if another bundle has aggregate at least C, the support inequality requires its price-valued change from the candidate to be nonnegative.

    At the case-1 prices, P=6/5, demands are 36/25 and16/25, expenditure is 6/5 and dispersion is their equally weighted sum26/25. Labor is YΔ/A=26/25. The index recursion reads1=(1/2)(6/5)+(1/2)(5/4)−1; the dispersion recursion gives(1/2)(6/5)²+(1/2)(5/4)−2=26/25. For general positive prices, X=(P(j)/P)1−ε has mean1; the strict Jensen inequality gives E Xε/(ε−1)≥1, equality only for constant X. CES aggregation values the composition of varieties, so the arithmetic average of their physical units is an input accounting quantity, not C.

  2. For p>0, objective F(p)=S₀p1−ε−S₁p−ε has derivative p−ε−1[εS₁−(ε−1)S₀p]. Its sole root μS₁/S₀ separates strict increase from strict decrease. As p↓0 the negative cost term dominates and F→−∞; as p→∞ F→0, while the candidate profit is positive. Hence this is a global unique maximum, without needing global concavity of F.

    The infinite sums are S₀=5/3,S₁=4/5 and p*=24/25. The true two-date sums are7/5 and16/25, giving p*=32/35. The omitted j≥2 tails are (4/15,4/25), since (2/5)²/(1−2/5)=4/15 and future cost is3/5. Adding them restores the infinite sums. A solver may truncate with an explicit tail/error bound, but dropping the tails and reporting the resulting ratio as exact changes the optimization problem.

  3. The index derivative is0=θ(ε−1)π+(1−θ)(1−ε)q*, so q*=θπ/(1−θ). Dispersion differentiation yields dΔt=θdΔt−1+θεπ−(1−θ)εq*=θdΔt−1. With dΔ₋₁=0, induction makes its first-order component zero. That is consistent with exact dispersion being second order for small normalized relative-price differences.

    With an independently specified positive dΔ₋₁=d, the solution is dΔt=θt+1d. Linearized labor is n=y−a+dΔ, since Δ̄=1. The inherited dispersion deviation is then a predetermined endogenous state, so the preceding two-jump-only root count does not describe this enlarged initial-condition problem without adjustment. Neither result permits setting exact Δ=1 along arbitrary inflation paths.

  4. Increasing Bt+1 by a nominal unit costs Qt/Pt consumption now and adds1/Pt+1 tomorrow. The derivative condition is QtCt−σ/Pt=βEt[Ct+1−σ/Pt+1], giving the stated Euler relation. Around R̄=1/β and zero inflation, its first-order form is σ(Ec′−c)=i−Eπ′. Use c=y=x+yn and rearrange to obtain the IS equation with rn=σEΔyn.

    For the new parameters, yn=(2/3)a=1/50. Expected natural growth is(2/3)(−1/5)(3/100)=−1/250; rn=-1/125. Productivity is high today but expected to revert. The natural real rate reflects expected consumption growth, not simply the sign of today’s productivity level. These are deviations around a deterministic steady state; the level rate includes ī and nonlinear uncertainty corrections are not computed.

  5. Substitute q*=θπ/(1−θ) into q*=(1−βθ)m+βθE(q*′+π′). The future coefficient becomes βθ/(1−θ), so division by θ/(1−θ) gives π=βEπ′+[(1−θ)(1−βθ)/θ]m. With m=(σ+φ)x this yields κ. At θ=3/4, λ=(1/4)(2/5)/(3/4)=2/15 and κ=4/15. This is 2/9 of the benchmark6/5. The curve is flatter under these maintained primitives; this is not an estimate of an empirical causal effect of price duration.

    At θ=0 all firms can reset, so desired markup directly fixes real marginal cost; the expression with1/θ is undefined. At θ=1 no firm resets, eliminating the reset optimization and changing the equilibrium restrictions; sending κ to zero does not prove that every result derived for0<θ<1 survives.

  6. The characteristic polynomial has T>2,D>1 and p(1) proportional to κ(φπ−1)+(1−β)φx. Complex conjugate roots have modulus√D>1. Real roots are positive; p(1)>0 puts both on the same side of1, while T>2 excludes the lower side. A negative p(1) places one root below and one above1; equality gives roots1,D. Thus strict positivity is necessary and sufficient under these sign restrictions.

    The active roots are3/2 and11/4; passive roots1/2 and13/4; boundary roots1 and11/4. For passive feedback, A=[[5/2,−1],[−3/2,5/4]] sends(1/2,1) to(1/4,1/2), proving the decaying family. At the boundary the Phillips condition for a constant path is(1−β)π=κx, giving x=π/6; IS and i=π then hold. The uniqueness class is uniformly bounded adapted rational-expectations processes driven by bounded fundamentals on the true filtration, including extra public signals if their objective conditional law is used. Iterated differences MnE dt+n vanish only with the stated continuation control. The claim does not cover all unbounded sunspot paths or exact nonlinear equilibria.

  7. The matrix is ((0,1/4),(-3/2,5/4)), with trace5/4 and determinant3/8. Its polynomial is(ℓ−1/2)(ℓ−3/4), so the roots are (1/2,3/4). Both directions decay. At zero fundamentals arbitrary small coefficients on their two independent eigenvectors generate bounded perfect-foresight paths. Since x and π are both jump variables with no prescribed initial values, those two stable directions mean two free initial choices, not a uniquely pinned stable allocation. The positive-inflation-coefficient shortcut failed because φx≥0 was dropped. The earlier trace/determinant inequalities were assumptions-dependent, not universal identities about all monetary rules.

  8. Substituting x=Xν,π=Hν into Phillips gives(1−βρ)H=κX. The IS relation is σ(1−ρ)X=−[φπH+φxX+1−ρH]; eliminating H gives X=−1/Dρ. Under the active rule andρ=1/2, H=2X andDρ=3, yielding x=−1/100,π=−1/50,i=−1/200. Expected inflation is−1/100, so the real-rate deviation is1/200. Expected gap growth is(ρ−1)x=1/200, matching σ=1.

    Underφπ=2, Dρ=4; expected next inflation is−3/400 and the real-rate deviation is 3/800. Expected gap growth is likewise3/800. For the iid case D₀=33/10; x=−1/110,π=−3/275,i=1/110 and expected next inflation is zero. Its real-rate deviation is 1/110=−x. All three outcomes contract demand relative to the natural allocation, even though the nominal rate has opposite signs across persistence specifications. Observing its sign alone does not identify ν without the structural rule, expectations and competing shocks.

  9. Adding rn to the rule cancels it in the IS equation, so f=0. The zero gap/inflation path solves the system. With both forward roots outside the unit circle, bounded homogeneous solutions satisfy zt=MnE zt+n→0, proving uniqueness. Output is y=yn=[(1+φ)/(σ+φ)]a and responds to productivity. Tracking a detrended series in place of this natural allocation can therefore implement a different feedback.

    Without the correcting subsidy, flexible pricing gives W/P=A/μ. Equating it toχYσ(Y/A)φ yields Ynaturalσ+φ=A1+φ/(χμ), whereas the efficient allocation satisfies Yefficientσ+φ=A1+φ/χ. Thus Ynatural/Yefficient=μ−1/(σ+φ)<1. Stabilizing the natural gap removes deviations from a distorted allocation; it is not a proof of social optimality. Funding a corrective subsidy requires the lump-sum taxes already specified; distortionary financing would require a new welfare analysis.

  10. Let a=φx+φπκ=6/5 and ī=−logβ. At zero continuation, the unfloored solution is x=r/(σ+a), π=κx and i=ar/(σ+a). It is feasible when r≥−ī(σ+a)/a; equality meets both regimes. The floor solution is x=(r+ī)/σ,π=κx,i=−ī and is consistent exactly on the other side. The threshold is -0.018425615731419325. At r=−0.02 the unfloored rate would be−0.01090909, below−ī; the floor must bind.

    At t=1 use x₁=r+ī andπ₁=κx₁. At t=0 the IS equation gives x₀=(2+κ)x₁ and Phillips givesπ₀=κ(β+2+κ)x₁. Both shadow rates lie below−ī, as case5 calculates. Given future values, the scalar piecewise equation has strictly increasing left side, proving each backward step unique and continuous at the threshold. Setting i=0 instead sets logR=ī>0, not logR=0. The selected zero continuation at date2 closes this experiment; without it, infinite-horizon expectations and regime selection raise additional questions.

  11. Direct multiplication verifies AM=I for M=[[10/33,−2/33],[4/11,8/11]]. Its row sums in absolute value are4/11 and12/11, so the ordinary∞-norm is not a contraction modulus below one. S=[[1,1],[−1,−6]] has inverse ((6/5,1/5),(-1/5,-1/5)). Its columns correspond to forward eigenvalues11/4 and3/2, so S−1MS=diag(4/11,2/3).

    For error d=z̃−z*, the residual definition gives dt=MEtdt+1+et. Conditional expectation is a nonexpansion in the supremum over histories of this norm. Iteration and boundedness give‖d‖S≤η∑(2/3)j=3η. Rows of S have absolute sums2 and7, yielding |Δx|≤6η and|Δπ|≤21η. At the supplied η, the bounds are (3/50000,21/100000). They are bounds on the linear solution, not forecasts of actual errors. If the expectation operator is misspecified, its discrepancy enters the residual budget; fitting the wrong transition law exactly provides no certificate for the intended one.

  12. Root and solution-class objection. Exercise7 hasφπ=3/2 but two stable roots and multiple bounded paths. The sign restrictions, rule timing, endogenous state count, objective expectations and boundedness class must accompany a determinacy claim. Tiny Euler errors alone do not check the Phillips relation, rule, branch feasibility or admissibility.

    Gap and measurement objection. Exercise4 has rising natural output but a negative natural-rate deviation. Output minus a trend need not equal y−yn. A fitted gap, Calvo duration or residual process needs an empirical measurement and identification argument; the original parameter examples supply none.

    Nonlinear and floor objection. Case5’s unconstrained solution violates the floor despite satisfying that unconstrained linear system. A correct branch and terminal selection are needed, and the zero continuation establishes only the finite conditional experiment. Price dispersion in case1 is4%, even though a first-order expansion from uniform prices removes its first derivative. A small linear residual is not an exact nonlinear error bound.

    Welfare and funding objection. Zero natural gap can stabilize a monopoly-distorted allocation if the subsidy is absent. If it is present, taxes must fund it. A rule comparison for one shock is not maximization of a stated welfare objective across feasible policies, especially with distributional effects or distortionary finance omitted. Household ownership, policy information and constraints all matter.

    Ten-point rubric. Award two points to each of the four objection groups: one for a concrete valid witness and one for the missing condition or evidence. Award one point for a coherent narrower claim and one for distinguishing a changed economic model from a numerical repair. A defensible replacement is: “For the specified first-order two-jump system, nonnegative feedbacks satisfying the proved inequality give one uniformly bounded rational-expectations solution; the reported shock comparison and finite-floor experiment are conditional on their stated laws and continuation. Nonlinear accuracy, causal fit and policy welfare require further evidence.” Other carefully delimited conclusions earn full credit; blanket approval or rejection does not.

8. Explain and retain the distinctions

Teach-back. Explain in four minutes why a resetter considers future costs, why exact dispersion can matter even when its first derivative vanishes, why forward roots outside the unit circle select jump variables, and why a falling nominal rate can accompany contractionary policy.

Benchmark answer. A nominal price may survive several dates, so the firm maximizes a survival-weighted stream and chooses a ratio of discounted cost and demand weights. CES relative-price differences require extra labor; the zero first derivative is an approximation property around uniform prices, not exact equality. With two freely chosen initial jump variables, bounded continuation excludes two explosive forward directions; passive or unit-root directions leave free bounded paths. Finally, policy changes expectations and endogenous feedback: case4’s nominal rate falls while expected inflation falls farther, raising the real rate and lowering the gap.

Delayed retention. After one week without the chapter: (1) write the funded subsidy accounts; (2) derive the two-variable determinacy margin and state its assumptions; (3) distinguish i=0 from logR=0; (4) give one reason a small simulation residual is not a welfare theorem.

Answer key. (1)T=τWN,D=PY−(1−τ)WN, so WN+D−T=PY. (2)κ(φπ−1)+(1−β)φx>0 underβ∈(0,1),σ,κ>0, nonnegative contemporaneous rule coefficients, two jumps and the stated bounded objective-expectations class. (3)i=logR−ī, so a zero nominal gross log rate means i=−ī; i=0 means the steady positive rate. (4)A residual may use a wrong shock law, ignore a binding regime, refer only to a linear model, omit terminal conditions or say nothing about an objective and feasible policy alternatives. Any one correctly explained reason suffices.

Next. Fiscal policy and sovereign debt introduces government intertemporal resources and fiscal-monetary interaction. The contemporaneously funded subsidy here deliberately carries no government debt. Adding fiscal liabilities, price-level fiscal backing or default changes the equilibrium problem; the two-jump monetary proof cannot be imported without recounting states, budgets and terminal restrictions.
